speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to table order in council P.C. 408 which proclaims the National Housing Act, 1954, as of Monday, March 22, 1954. I am also tabling a copy of the regulations under P.C. 409 as well as P.C. 410 setting forth the interest rates. The maximum rate of interest for insured mortgage loans has been established at 5J per cent. In respect of rental insurance loans, the same rate applies. The interest rate for limited dividend companies remains unchanged at 3 f per cent. The maximum level of loans for home ownership has been established at $12,800 for a single house and $15,300 for a duplex exclusive of the insurance premium. Regulations for the operation of the act have been established and the form of mortgage deeds has been determined. There is provision that prepaid monthly tax instalments in the hands of the approved lenders shall bear interest at the savings account rate of the chartered banks. Explanatory leaflets and forms are being distributed so that the new legislation may be operative next Monday morning.

speakerposition: stagedirection

subtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE AT WASHINGTON
speechtext:
May
I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he will give the house some report on the conference held at Washington this week between representatives of the Canadian government and representatives of the United States government, and in particular tell the house what agreements or undertakings were entered into on behalf of either of the countries with respect to trade in any of its aspects?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE AT WASHINGTON
speechtext:
I am glad to take this opportunity to tell hon. members something about the meeting. I consider it a very important meeting indeed. I believe it is the first occasion on which four senior cabinet ministers of the United States have met with four members of the Canadian government to discuss matters of common interest in the field of economics. I think that the meetings were summed up very well by the communique issued at their conclusion, which I have not seen published in full in the Canadian press. I suggest that the reading of that communique may give my hon. friend the answers that he requires. It reads as follows:
The first meeting of the joint United States-Cana-dian committee on trade and economic affairs was held in Washington on the 16th of March. The United States was represented by Hon. John Foster Dulles, Secretary of State, Hon. George M. Humphrey, Secretary of the Treasury, Hon. Ezra Taft Benson, Secretary of Agriculture and Hon. Sinclair Weeks, Secretary of Commerce. Canada was represented by Right Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Trade and Commerce and Defence Production, Right Hon, James G. Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture, Hon. Douglas Abbott, Minister of Finance-

subtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE AT WASHINGTON
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE AT WASHINGTON
speechtext: Did I slip?

subtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE AT WASHINGTON
speechtext: Years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCE AT WASHINGTON
speechtext:
I continue:
-and Hon. L. B. Pearson, Secretary of State for External Affairs. In addition to the members of the joint committee, Governor Adams, the assistant to the President, the Hon. Douglas Stuart, United States ambassador to Canada and Dr. Gabriel Hauge, economic assistant to the president, participated in the discussions.
The purpose of the meeting was to provide an opportunity for United States and Canadian ministers to examine the trade and economic problems that are common to both countries.
The ministers noted that the flow of trade between Canada and the United States is greater than that between any other two countries. They discussed

various aspects of present trade relations and agreed on the desirability of avoiding any action which would interfere with this trade from which the two countries derive such great benefits.
Since the common economic problems of Canada and the United States can be solved with greatest success in a world where the volume of trade is steady and increasing and where exchange arrangements are of a kind to facilitate such growth, consideration was given through the discussions to the need for action towards freer trade and payments on a broad front. It was agreed that few things would contribute more to the well-being and stability of the free nations of the world than a forward move in this direction. The need for such progress seemed all the greater at a time when many western countries are faced with the necessity of supporting effective defence programs over a long period.
The United States and Canadian ministers found encouragement in many of the economic developments that have taken place over the past year. They noted that the gold and dollar reserves of other countries generally have been rising; that there has been a marked improvement in the internal economic stability of many countries; and that these favourable developments have made possible some relaxation of import restrictions. Nevertheless, it was agreed that the recovery to economic health has not progressed equally for all countries. What is needed, it was concluded, is the creation of a more flexible system of trade and payments throughout the world which would offer greater resilience to changing circumstances and which would contribute dynamically towards rising standards of living. It was agreed that much of the necessary preparation for such an advance has already been accomplished by the work of the commission on foreign economic policy in the United States, by the proposals of the commonwealth economic conference, and by discussions within the organization for European economic co-operation.
In the meantime, it was agreed that it is essential that pressing, but possibly temporary, economic problems should not be solved by expedients which might make more difficult the advance on a broad front that was held to be necessary. One immediate problem which received close consideration was that raised by the accumulation of large agricultural surpluses. Special incentives and favourable weather conditions have operated in varying degrees to enlarge these surpluses. The ministers of both countries recognized that if surpluses were to be disposed of without regard to the impact on normal trade great damage might be done not only to the commerce of Canada and the United States but also to the world economy. The ministers reaffirmed that it is the continuing policy of their respective governments, in disposing of agricultural surpluses abroad, to consult with interested countries and not to interfere with normal commercial marketings. They stated that it is their settled intention that any extraordinary measures that might be adopted to reduce surpluses should result in greater consumption and should augment, and not displace, normal quantities of agricultural products entering into world trade.
In advancing toward a freer system of world trade and payments, it was agreed that existing international organizations would continue to play an important role. The valuable work already done by the international monetary fund, the international bank and the contracting parties of the general agreement on tariffs and trade was recognized. Ministers noted with satisfaction the arrangements which have recently been made within the fund to enable its resources to be used more effectively. Acknowledgment was also made of the useful service that has been performed by GATT in developing a code of commercial conduct and in
Inquiries of the Ministry providing a forum where multilateral tariff agreements could be negotiated and where the problems of commercial policy could be discussed.
It was appreciated that it is for countries whose currencies are now inconvertible to decide when and under what circumstances they might wish to make them convertible. It was also realized that enlightened economic policies on the part of the United States and Canada will materially contribute to establishing and maintaining broader freedom of trade and payments throughout the world. Because of the importance of that objective, the United States and Canadian ministers warmly welcomed the evidence of a desire in many countries to take decisive steps toward the restoration of a broad area of convertibility, and expressed a willingness to do their part to help in making such a movement successful.
The discussions at this meeting of the joint committee were marked by the friendliness and candor which are characteristic of relations between the two countries. At the invitation of the Canadian ministers the second meeting of the joint committee will be held in Ottawa.

My first reaction after reading the editorial as a whole was that it did not deserve or require comment. But I think perhaps, out of courtesy to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, that I might offer this comment.
One of the functions of the present inquiry into loss leader selling is to consider the large number of complaints that have been received about price reductions in the sales of many nationally advertised goods. I feel, therefore, that these complaints contradict rather conclusively the main contention of the Financial Times editorial.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this bill passes, and' in order to make the position absolutely clear, I wish to make a brief statement.
Gold is money. Money is of value because it is freely convertible into goods and services, by direct exchange. For gold to fulfil its major function, it must be made freely exchangeable into goods or services by the same simple operation based on agreement between buyer and seller. This is the essential qualification of the free market. It is the basic law of the capitalist or free economy.
It is my contention that the problem of gold will not be solved until this is brought about.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

I therefore do so. Section 53 of the Immigration Act, which is chapter 325 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, is as follows:
Where an offence under this act or the regulations has been committed by a corporation and whether or not the corporation has been prosecuted or convicted, every person who at the time of the commission of the offence was a director or officer of tMr. Macdonnell.l
the corporation is guilty of the like offence and is liable on conviction to the punishment provided for the offence upon proof that the act or omission constituting the offence took place with his knowledge or consent, or that he failed to exercise due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence.
I have not been able to check it myself, Mr. Chairman, but I am advised that that section is exactly similar in terms to clause 20 of this bill.
On the question of the suggestion that the word "knowingly" or similar words be inserted in the final provision of this particular clause, I think I should say to the committee that, in connection with offences under this act-as is true in connection with offences under acts such as the Immigration Act-the proof of the element of knowledge is one that can in certain instances be particularly difficult. This matter was given careful consideration, and it was felt that there would be unreasonable and unnecessary difficulty in bringing to justice persons who were in fact guilty of offences under the act if the element of proof of actual knowledge were added to the already rather reasonable requirements that the crown prove a lack of due diligence to prevent. The law officers and the crown felt that that was sufficient protection to anyone who was not guilty of an offence; that it provided a proper element of defence; that to the requirement of proof of due diligence the addition of proof of actual knowledge was an undue burden of proof to impose on the crown and that it would contribute to evasions of the act that should not be permitted to occur.

speechtext:
We have not an amendment worked out, Mr. Chairman, but I wonder whether the minister and his assistant would consider the possibility of confining the effect and application of this section so far as the last two lines are concerned, starting with the words "or that he failed to exercise due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence", to a case of the export of strategic materials? I think no objection could be taken to the proposition that where a person gets a permit for the export of a strategic material which it is desired to prevent from falling into the hands of potential enemies, he there has an absolute duty thrust upon him to ensure that it does not fall into the hands of those potential enemies.
Therefore the provision of these words in imposing the duty of due diligence on him is reasonable, but in the case of a corporation engaged in ordinary commerce within Canada and, let us say, securing an import permit, it is well known that directors do not all pay close attention to the details of

the business. Quite often they are there for the effect of their names and their general business knowledge but do not participate actively in the detailed running of the business and to impose that burden of diligence and supervision upon directors with respect to the detailed activities of the firm within Canada is unreasonable. Therefore I put this proposition forward. Might it not be worked out to confine the effect of these words to the case of a corporation obtaining a permit for the export of strategic materials?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ACCOUNT FOR REPLACEMENT OF GOVERNMENT PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the resolution stage we had a fairly pertinent discussion about this bill but probably a few additional remarks would be in order. The object of the bill is to establish a fire losses replacement account and to authorize advances from the account for the restoration, the rebuilding or repair of property under the administration or control of departments and certain agency crown corporations that has been destroyed or damaged through fire.
The purpose to be served by this measure can be stated very briefly. It is to ensure, when a fire loss occurs and the replacement or repair of property destroyed or damaged is urgently and immediately required and there is not sufficient money available in the appropriation for the service suffering loss, that authority and funds will be available, subject to the approval of the treasury board, to proceed with the repair or replacement without delay.
To illustrate, a government hospital, a customs office, a fish hatchery, a garage housing valuable automotive equipment may be destroyed by fire and must be replaced immediately if essential services are to be restored with the least interruption. The balance available in the appropriation for the particular service concerned, which would not ordinarily include provision for

Fire Losses Replacement Account such a contingency, may not be sufficient for the purpose. Under the proposed bill the money required for the replacement or the restoration of the building or the replacement of the equipment or supplies might, with the approval of the treasury board, be advanced temporarily from the fire losses replacement account on the understanding that the account would be recouped subsequently by charges to the appropriation for the service concerned.
There is authority in the Financial Administration Act for the use of special governor general warrants when accidents happen to public works and buildings and expenditures for their repair or renewal are urgently required, but as hon. members are aware this authority is available only when parliament is not in session or is under adjournment sine die or for a period of two weeks or more.
It has also been the practice in recent years to include in the annual appropriations for the Department of Finance a vote for miscellaneous minor and unforeseen contingencies. However, this is limited in amount. $1,500,000 is provided in the estimates for the current year and only $1 million in the estimates for 1954-55, and the vote is intended to cover the contingency requirements of all departments. Consequently, if a major fire were to occur it might not be sufficient to provide funds for the replacement of the fire loss and to meet the other unforeseen demands that might arise during the course of the year. It is for this reason that it has seemed advisable to provide a special account to deal solely with fire losses.
It is proposed that advances from the account shall be subject to the approval of the treasury board, that they shall not exceed an aggregate of $5 million at any time, and that they shall be recovered subsequently by charges to parliamentary appropriations for the service suffering the loss.
The account is essentially an arrangement to ensure that when fires do occur essential services can be restored with a minimum of interruption by providing the means to make advances for the immediate replacement of the facilities lost or damaged.

subtopic: MEASURE TO REQUIRE EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is described as an act to provide equal pay for equal work for women. It contains a recital which reads in this way:
Whereas it is desirable to enact a measure to prevent discrimination against women in respect of their employment by reason of their sex and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, to ensure that women will be paid at the same rates as men for similar or comparable work.
I deem it a great privilege to second the motion of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) for the second reading of this bill. When it was last discussed on March 2, there was a speech by the hon. member, followed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg). I thought he was under some considerable difficulty and embarrassment in trying to make out a case against the bill. He was not very convincing in his arguments, and summed up his position in this way, as reported at page 2594 of Hansard:
Again I say there is a difference between attempting to bring about a remedy by law and having it carried out by collective bargaining on the one hand, and probably the more potent weapon of education on the other. It is because I am not convinced of the necessity or the desirability of trying to enforce such a law within those industries which are subject to federal labour jurisdiction that I reluctantly find I shall have to vote against my hon. friend's bill.
Now, let us take a look at the objection that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) has to the bill. In the first place he intimates that these rates should be covered by collective bargaining. Earlier in his speech he pointed out that some agreements negotiated under collective bargaining contain equal pay clauses. He went on to say:
Some agreements contain equal pay clauses, and others simply carry out the principle of equal pay by establishing a rate for the job which is the same whether the job is done by a man or a woman.

Therefore it is obvious that the position is not going to be greatly improved by collective bargaining and I do not believe the minister was sound in opposing the bill on that ground. In fact, he went on to point out that the federal civil service commission follows the second course, namely, that of treating all jobs as equal no matter whether they happen to be occupied by a man or a woman.
His second ground was that this problem should be met by education. That is a very indefinite way to meet this problem. There has already been sufficient education of the people of Canada for them to know whether or not they believe in equal pay for women, and I am afraid the minister's suggestion that we should turn this problem over to someone unnamed to bring about more education was just an evasion of the question posed by this bill.
I believe this legislation is very timely. It was pointed out the other day by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) that there is similar legislation in the provinces of Ontario, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. I hold in my hand a bill which was passed last fall by the British Columbia legislature. It is described as: "An act to ensure fair remuneration to female employees" and is cited as "The Equal Pay Act". The key words are to get the same pay "for the same work done in the same establishment". These key words are not exactly the same as the ones contained in the bill now before us, but I think they are of a similar nature and would be construed in the same way.
In British Columbia we have had a further move along this line recently. In February of this year the Vancouver city school board adopted the principle of equal pay for women teachers. I hold in my hand a press clipping from the Vancouver Province reporting that decision, and it says that the big factor this year in the negotiations of the pay for the year-
-was the principle of equal pay for equal work for the 1,100 women teachers in the city.
Therefore the principle has been accepted in our city, and I understand it has also been accepted in many other parts of this nation.
I would point out to the minister that just last year he himself sponsored a similar bill. I refer to the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, chapter 19 of the statutes of 1952-53. It is described as "an act to prevent discrimination in regard to employment and membership in trade unions by reason of race, national origin, colour or religion." That act received the unanimous support of hon. members. It is in much the same terms
Industrial Status of Women as the bill brought in by the hon. member for Hamilton West. Enforcement is based on a complaint system and I suggest to the minister and to my fellow members that the two bills are very much alike.
Last year the minister was full of enthusiasm for putting on the statute books of Canada a bill preventing discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour or religion; but this year he refuses to support a bill which would wipe out discrimination by reason of sex. Frankly, there is great inconsistency in the two stands taken by him.
You see, Mr. Speaker, the main purpose of a bill such as that which was passed last year, known as the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, is to set a standard. Its purpose is not to put people in jail or have them fined or to make trouble across this land. The main purpose is to set up a standard, and it was on that basis that hon. members approved the legislation last year.
We have had other examples. I refer the minister to the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act. He has always been very much interested in legislation for the war veterans of this country and, as he knows, this act to which I am now referring was passed to help the veterans who returned to Canada to get back their old jobs. It has been effective. I do not think there could have been a more effective piece of legislation to enable the young men and young women who were demobilized to get back their jobs or to get reasonable employment.
The act contains drastic provisions for dealing with those employers who break the law. And yet, I understand from the minister's own department that less than half a dozen prosecutions have been laid under the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act. Actually there have been so few prosecutions that his department could not tell me just how many there had been, but after scratching their heads quite a while they thought that perhaps there may have been from two to five. There has been just that little need to take punitive action under that particular legislation.
The bill brought in by the hon. member for Hamilton West is of exactly the same type. I doubt whether there would be many prosecutions under it if it were to become law. There might be one or two. Probably there would be very few, because Canadian employers have shown down through the years that all they need to know is what the legislation is that stands on the statute books and they are prepared to abide by it. That has been shown only too clearly by literally

Industrial Status of Women thousands of employers under this Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, and I am quite sure that the same results are going to flow from the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act which we passed last year. The Canadian people obey the law. Every hon. member who has had much experience here will agree with me when I say that once a law is placed on the statute books there are not very many Canadians who try to break it. The public reaction is: That is the law and it is reasonable, and we are going to abide by it. I feel quite sure that the result would be the same if this equal pay for equal work for women act were placed on the statute books.
This is not a bill on which the government stands or falls. The private members of the government party are in the position to vote for this bill, believing it is a proper measure, without, by that vote, endangering the government. I am quite sure the Minister of Labour will agree with me in that assertion. I see him nodding his head and therefore he does agree.
I would urge hon. members of this house to support this measure for the reason that it will set up a nation-wide standard. We believe that equal pay for women is a practice which should be followed. The government of Canada has shown approval of that principle for many years by treating its own civil servants in that manner. Now, let us complete the job by setting up, through this bill, a standard for the entire nation.

That indicates that the unions recognize the need for paying women at the same rate as men. The minister also pointed out that 3 per cent indicated that they favoured a discrepancy in pay. One question immediately enters my mind. I wonder what

The minister also said that the major congresses had not made representations to the government in this respect. Possibly the reason for their not having made representations in this respect is that the congresses feel, as so many of us do, that this is a provincial matter. However, it has apparently entered the federal field and therefore it should be dealt with at a federal level.
I support the spirit of this measure and I would suggest its adoption, although at the same time I recognize the difficulties involved in trying to implement it. There are certain reasons why I believe this bill should be passed. The first is that many firms today pay women less than they do men for doing exactly the same type of work. For example, in our retail marketing a delivery boy gets more money than a girl at the cash register who keeps punching the keys all day long. That is rather unfortunate, in my opinion, because she probably has much more responsibility, handling thousands of dollars during a month, than the delivery boy who delivers a few dollars' worth of groceries.
In the civil service we know there is no discrimination whatsoever. We recognize that men and women are equal. As regards the teaching profession, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) indicated that women are just as capable as men in that particular profession. I would go so far as to say that in many instances they have proved far superior to men in the teaching profession.
Certain other industries have recognized that women are just as capable as men, and do just as good a job. There is no sound reason, as far as I can see, for not giving women equal pay. The minister said he had received no recommendations in favour of this legislation. I wonder if he has had representations to the effect that this legislation should not be put into effect, or if anyone has come to the government and said, "Please pass this bill but with the provision that women should be paid less than men."
Long ago Mrs. Pankhurst recognized the need to give women the vote. Long ago we recognized that they were capable of exercising that vote, and I am quite sure each of the men here feel that women were probably responsible for putting them in the position they now occupy.

Women have proved their superiority in many fields. We do not find very many men acting as telephone operators, and I do not know of a single instance where a man is employed punching a cash register in the supermarkets we have in the city, or in any other city I have been in. I know the girl at the cash register probably enhances the attractiveness of the store.

An hon. member says, "hear, hear". Possibly the reason she is employed as a cash register girl, if I may coin the phrase, is that she is most capable of punching the keys and can do it more rapidly than a man. In a case like that we should recognize that a girl should be paid the same as a man, if a man were employed to do that type of work.
The unions a long time ago advocated this sort of legislation, and have long recognized its value. It is quite obvious that if women were not as capable as men they would not be employed. Women have proved their worth and ability during the course of two world wars. During those wars thousands of women in this country were employed in industry, and I would go so far as to say that if women had not been there we probably would have lost those wars. It was only through their efforts that the boys in the front lines were given the supplies they so badly needed.
Industry should repay women for keeping the front lines supplied, and the best way of doing that is to pay them their dollar's worth if they are capable of doing the job as well as a man.
There is one other reason why I am so particularly happy to support this measure. That is because it adopts a great Social Credit principle. That principle is that the way to make the poor richer is to raise the level of their wages to that of the higher paid workers. We do not advocate taking from the rich and giving to the poor. We believe wages should be raised to the point where they are on a level with the wages received by the better paid workers. I have found, and I speak with some authority having a family of four girls, that it costs just as much to clothe and keep women as it does to keep men. It costs just as much to clothe them and to keep them as it does to clothe and to keep a man.

By an equal pay act we would certainly be able to equalize our costs of labour and make our competitor become an honest competitor at least in so far as the price of labour is concerned.
The effect of this legislation, if it were to become an act, would be possibly threefold. The first effect might be illustrated in this way, if others felt as did a young lady I happened to meet in the corridor as I was coming down to the chamber. One of the young ladies asked me what I was getting prepared to speak on. I said, "The equal pay act". Her first reaction was, "Hurrah, that means the 40-hour week". Apparently the girls are not working the 40-hour week in this institution. While that feature is not embodied in the bill itself-I refer to the hours of labour-you can see that women are not opposed to it on that particular basis.
There would be a natural increase in unemployment among the women at first. The employers would naturally say this; "If I have to pay a woman the same price as I am going to pay a man, I am going to get a man for this job"; and out goes the woman. That may be the first repercussion. It would possibly be an unfortunate one. But if that male employee was not as capable of producing articles as was a woman or was not as capable of doing the job properly, he would naturally enough be replaced by a woman at a later time; and instead of our Minister of Labour having such a fine steady graph line for the employment of females over a period of years as compared with the one for men employees, he would have
3170	HOUSE OF
Industrial Status of Women fluctuations in the women's line of employment comparable with that for men at the present time.
Then there is one third possible effect. It will probably mean that the male employment situation will be much improved. We have had several representations, I believe, in the corridors by the various labour groups and nearly every one of them has strongly demanded more employment, that the government find employment for them; and in nearly every instance it was a case of employment for male employees. That situation would be naturally improved if the other argument that I proposed a moment ago were followed through. It would have a far-reaching effect upon our morale, I dare say. If the housewife did not prove herself to be as efficient as the male employee, she would find herself unemployed and would be back at home doing housework. Whether or not that is a desirable thing I am not going to discuss at this time. However, I will say this. If she does prove herself to be a better worker than the male, she will become the breadwinner for the family and we shall find the husband at home doing the chores.

subtopic: MEASURE TO REQUIRE EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me much pleasure to rise to support this bill. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) for seeing to it that this was the first bill that appeared on the order paper for discussion by members when we came here for this present session of parliament.
I am sorry that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) is unable or unwilling to support it.
I am happy, however, that we have not had many speakers on the government side who have offered opposition.
The Financial Times is about the only publication I have run across that seems to be opposed to this sort of legislation. In the Financial Times of March 12 I find an article under the name "Tempus". It reads a good deal like the writing by Austin Cross. I think the kindest thing I can say is that the writer must have had a deadline to meet and very little to write about when he used up valuable space with this material. He said:
. . . far too many secretaries have far too much to say and far too much to do with the .administration.
He was speaking about the women private secretaries in the government administration here. The article continues:
Yes, and put me down as saying that there are far too many women holding down jobs that should be held down by men . . .
Once upon a time, cabinet ministers here appointed a male secretary. Now far too many females have the jobs.
[Mr. Hahn.)

Then further on:
It is not that the women are not efficient, but they are, for the most part, of a good stenography level. This business of being a political secretary to the boss is too much for most of them. For the most part women have no political savvy.
Mr. Speaker, we have the misfortune to have in the House of Commons only four women out of a total membership of 265. I think that is a reflection on the women of Canada. I think it is unfortunate for parliament. The four women are making an outstanding contribution. In addition to the four who are here now, so far as I know we have had only five other women who have been in parliament since confederation. First, there was Miss Macphail, then Mrs. Black, Mrs. Nielsen, Mrs. Casselman and Mrs. Strum.
To come back to the comments made by the writer of this article-Tempus, whoever that is-may I say that I think the government is to be commended for choosing some women to hold down the responsible positions of private secretaries. My telephone directory informs me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) all have women private secretaries. I notice that there are not any women holding down jobs as deputy ministers. While waiting to speak I was looking through the estimates and I am now prompted to wonder whether the reason we get some women private secretaries is partly the result of the fact that the salaries offered for private secretaries are not high enough to attract males with the qualifications for doing that type of work.
I was under the impression that a private secretary had nearly as much responsibility as a deputy minister, but in some cases the salaries offered to private secretaries are about a third of those paid to deputy ministers. I think that the business of securing executive assistants probably has given cabinet ministers a chance to get on their staff people who are earning more than private secretaries. But I am sure that members of all political parties who have done business with the offices of the ministers would agree that no one should throw bricks at private secretaries merely because they are women. I think it is childish for anyone in the middle of the twentieth century to suggest that for the most part women have no political savvy. I think you might as well say that men have no political savvy.
I also think that to handicap individuals because they are women and make it impossible for them to occupy the most important

positions in the country because they are women just cannot be justified in this day and age.
I am glad that the hon. member tor Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) has examined the bills that have been passed in Ontario, British Columbia and Saskatchewan and has decided that the most attractive legislation has been passed in my province where the wording is equal pay "for similar or comparable work". That is the wording we find in the present bill. I do not want to be in the position of talking out the bill, but I could not let this opportunity pass without registering my protest against the sentiments expressed by "Tempus" and objecting to the opinions expressed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) who apparently cannot support this legislation. I would hope that before very much longer the government will be prepared to go along with the governments of Ontario, Saskatchewan and British Columbia and make legislation such as has been proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton West one of the laws of this country.

subtopic: MEASURE TO REQUIRE EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that we should avoid labour legislation of a compulsory nature that would interfere with the free rights of collective bargaining. However, I do not think this measure falls within that classification. Rather, this is a matter of the basic rights of human beings, be they male or female. I appreciate what the minister has said regarding the use, or perhaps I should say lack of use, that has been made of this type of legislation where it is in effect. The records show that very little use has been made of it in the two provinces where it has been in operation for any length of time. I understand that the British Columbia legislation was enacted only this year. In thirteen states of the United States there is a similar type of legislation, although it varies a little between states. Here again very little use has been made of it.
I discussed this matter with some of the people in the women's bureau in the United States and asked them what they thought the solution was. They felt that collective bargaining was the answer in those cases where women do belong to unions. But the unfortunate thing about women workers is that a great number of them-I do not know whether or not a majority-do not belong to unions. Therefore the type of legislation proposed in the bill now before us, under which the complaint is laid before the legislative body, seems to be about the only answer to the problem. But the legislation is simply not used where it is in effect.
19, 1954
Industrial Status of Women
When this bill was first mentioned in the press last December I was very much interested in reading an article in the Evening Citizen of December 4 headed "Equal Pay for Women Teachers". They were talking about Ottawa women teachers. The Ontario legislation providing equal pay for equal work for women has been in effect for something like two years and it is a very good act. It is very clear and simple. Yet Ottawa women teachers had asked the school board for equal pay and had been refused. The article goes on to point out that letters were sent to the board from the business and professional women's club and also from the university women's club begging the board to give the women teachers equal pay.
That is a very strange thing because I think I can say without fear of contradiction that school teachers in the province of Ontario at least-I am familiar with this province-have one of the strongest organizations that can be found anywhere. Just one teacher needed to bring this matter before the proper authorities of the provincial government, or a group of them, and yet they did not do so. I am not suggesting they were weak because they did not or that they should have done so. I do not know the circumstances. I can imagine many reasons why they did not.
The chairman of the school board, a lady, stated at the time that they simply could not afford it at this time. Perhaps the Ottawa lady teachers had lengthy discussions with the board and agreed with them or maybe they subsequently got what they wanted. I do not know, although I have watched the newspapers. But there was the situation. They had the law and they did not use it. I simply mention this to bear out some of the points raised by the minister.
An amusing thing happened at the time this article appeared in the paper. There was also a press report covering the presentation of the bill by the hon. member for Hamilton West. During that same week end I met several Ottawa people who said, "Won't it be nice when that bill goes through? School teachers in Ottawa will be able to get the same amount of money". It is a very strange thing, but it does not seem to matter how many times you try to tell people that the federal government cannot interfere with the rights of provincial governments with respect to labour disputes. Nor would the passing of this bill have any effect at all on the school teachers or, indeed, the majority of women workers in the province of Ontario. If the bill were passed a very limited number of women workers would benefit from it in any way. I was interested to hear what the

Industrial Status of Women minister said when he spoke on March 2. He said, as reported at page 2594 of Hansard:
. . . the four great national labour organizations have now made their annual presentations to the government and, although they have many women in their membership, have not recommended that such a bill be passed within the federal jurisdiction. I feel it is probably equally significant that the national council of women, in making their recommendations to the government, did not mention this matter.
The minister went on to say:
Before advocating federal legislation in this field I think I should like to know that a specific problem existed in the industries coming within federal jurisdiction, and that it was serious enough to warrant intervention. I would want to feel that the problem appeared capable of being remedied by law. So far I do not think there has been enough evidence of such a specific problem or of the fact that this is the remedy for it.
I am very happy to learn that we are to have a women's bureau. The minister has expressed himself as wanting to have all problems affecting women workers investigated. I am hoping that we will have a first-class women's bureau functioning very soon and that when the government does present legislation it will not only take care of this problem but will also lead the way in improving other working conditions of women.
I do not know how any legislation can take care of what I consider the most serious problem, and that is the lack of opportunity for women. There are not too many women who are suffering from a difference in pay, but there are a great many who are suffering from lack of opportunity. I feel that improvement in that direction can only be made by organized groups of employees.
I do not know how any government could help to take care of that situation.
I cannot dispute the statements made by the minister that the passing of this bill would mean very little to women employees under the jurisdiction of this government, because we not only recognize the principle but we practise it. Nevertheless, I do believe that the principle involved is of such basic importance to all women it should be written into the statutes of Canada. For that reason,
I must support the bill.

speechtext:
Before we deal with the items of the estimates I should like to put on record a few statistics and a general review of the mineral industry in Canada. I shall do this rather fully because our "summary of activities", the report distributed by the department to members of parliament each year, is not yet available from the printers.
This house has listened for many days this session to the disciples of blue ruin, predicting a depressing future for this country, growing unemployment and general decline. Mr. Chairman, we in Canada need never look back if we rise to the challenge of applying the great sources of energy we possess to the development of our national industrial structure. Nowhere else in the world today do 15 million people in one nation possess the heritage that is the lot of the Canadian people.
Not only does this nation have a remarkable heritage of mineral wealth but it also has proven sources of energy supply required to develop our natural resources. Our oil, natural gas, coal and electricity and in coming years perhaps atomic energy, are the keys to the unlocking of our great storehouse of minerals and our natural resources generally. One task facing us today is to develop these sources of energy and their distribution to areas of Canada where the energy can be most effectively used.
Mining in Canada in 1953 gave every evidence of a flourishing industry. Despite lower base metal prices, and labour disputes in two of the country's biggest camps, a new
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys high of $1,331 million was recorded in the value of mineral output, an increase of $46 million over 1952 and almost three times that of a decade ago. Over 128,500 men were employed in mines and quarries in 1953 at wages and salaries totalling $435 million.
Crude petroleum with an output valued at $198 million became Canada's No. 1 mineral, replacing gold which, after 25 years as the leading mineral, dropped to fourth place with a production valued at $139 million. Nickel at $161 million was second and copper at $151 million was third.
The sharp decline in lead and zinc prices brought about the closing down of several marginal producers particularly in British Columbia, and a substantial cutback in the production of zinc by Canada's largest producer.
As Canada is the leading exporter of the principal non-ferrous base metals much depends upon the export market particularly in United States. During the past year the question of tariffs on imports of base metals into United States has been widely discussed in that country. Canada has participated in some of these discussions, and it is hoped that a decision favourable to our base metal industry will be arrived at soon.
The outstanding feature of the year in the Canadian mineral industry, however, was the intensive and widespread exploratory and development activity that was carried out in the territories and in every province except Prince Edward Island. This activity resulted in, among other things, the bringing in of such new mines as the Eldorado Mining and Refining ace-fay uranium property in the Beaverlodge area of northern Saskatchewan, the Lynn Lake nickel-copper property in northern Manitoba, the Cassiar asbestos property in northern British Columbia and a copper-gold property in the Chibougamau area of Quebec, the first producer in that area. Much progress was made in the several large-scale projects under way such as that of Quebec-Labrador iron ore field into which the 360-mile railway has been virtually completed and from which ore is expected to be shipped by late summer, and at the Gaspe copper deposits which are to be brought in late this year.
An idea of the intensity of exploration, which proved greater in 1953 than in any other year in the history of Canadian mining, may be had from the preliminary estimate of over 130,000 claims staked during the year. This is a 216 per cent increase over 1952. The outstanding example was in New Brunswick, the scene of the Bathurst find, where some 41,000 claims were staked in 1953 compared with only 1,600 in 1952.
3176	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
Oil, natural gas, iron ore and uranium proved to be the major newsmakers in 1953. Oil production rose to 81 million barrels, compared with 61 million barrels in 1952. The industry spent some $365 million in the search for oil and discovered light crude oil in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and new major fields in Alberta.
The development of the petroleum and natural gas resources in western Canada in the last seven years has been so spectacular that they could not have been foreseen by even the most optimistic enthusiast. The initial stages caught the attention of the public and made headlines in the press, so that it seemed to many that suddenly, without preparation, great resources had been uncovered. This is not so. Back of these discoveries are years of patient toil on the part of many scientists and engineers. Through the years they have provided the fundamental knowledge on which the recent development is based.
The land subdivision of the early settlement years, done by the dominion land surveyors, together with the precise level and triangulation surveys of the geodetic survey, were the foundation in western Canada for the base maps formerly prepared under the department of the interior of the federal government, then under the geological survey, and now under the surveys and mapping branch of mines and technical surveys. Without adequate maps no resource development is possible in a systematic manner because each base map becomes the working tool of the geologists and geophysicists, under whose direction and guidance most exploratory programs are planned and carried out.
The foundations in the preparatory work for the successful development of petroleum and natural gas were laid by geologists of the geological survey of Canada. The names of Dawson, McConnell, Dowling and many others are famous in the interpretation of the geological features of western Canada. The reports of these men-the great geological pioneers of the plains, foothills and mountains-are still in great demand because of their clear exposition of the regional geological features based on their accurate observations.
Since about the beginning of this century the geological survey of Canada has each year had several parties in western Canada mapping geological features. The younger men of today on our staff are performing work just as important as the pioneers of yesterday, even though it is mostly of a more detailed nature. There now is an exceedingly


large amount of new information made available daily from the drilling of wells. The collection of this is a tremendous task for which we have a small staff in our Calgary office who, even though they cannot hope to keep pace in the complete correlation of all the data, are assisting in the development by making it available for the use of other geologists in the employ of the various oil companies.
It would be difficult to assess the value of this work. But certainly the combined efforts, not only of those in private enterprise, but also those in the employ of the various provincial governments of western Canada, as well as the federal government, are such that in relation to oil and gas discoveries the major problems have now suddenly become those of marketing, because of the great volume of riches that has been so rapidly revealed.
To summarize briefly the more recent developments is almost impossible because of the magnitude and significance of the results. For a time in the early part of 1953, it appeared that there would be a slackening in the discovery rate, but by the end of the year some really remarkable discoveries had been made. Among these may be cited the Roselea field in Manitoba, the Smiley field in Saskatchewan, and the Pembina and Sturgeon Lake fields in Alberta. New gas developments in northeast British Columbia assure more than adequate reserves for the West-coast Transmission line now planned to Vancouver and the Pacific northwest united states.
Of all the fields, Pembina is beyond doubt the largest, and recent estimates have placed the reserves at 800 million to 950 million barrels in this one field alone, with a possibility that the number of wells that ultimately will be drilled on 80 acre spacing will be equal in number to the 4,600 presently producing oil wells in the whole of Alberta. Recently in one week alone there were seven new discoveries of oil and gas in western Canada of which two were in Manitoba, one in Saskatchewan, three in Alberta, and one in British Columbia.
Although it is too early to assess the complete value of these, the one in Saskatchewan in the Estevan area is of very great importance in that the well yielded not only large volumes of gas but, in addition, a high volume of light crude oil. One of the Alberta discoveries in the area west and north of Didsbury also seems to be highly important, showing a thick porous section in the Missis-sippian from which the oil and gas in Turner valley was produced.

As far as the gas reserves are concerned, in the last year these have been increasing at an unprecedented rate and there is so much now beyond what Alberta can use in the next 30 years that there appears little doubt adequate reserves will be provided for the Trans-Canada gas line by the Alberta petroleum and natural gas conservation board.
As is well known, oil pipe lines have been built both east and west from Alberta. There is the Interprovincial pipe line, first built to Superior, Wisconsin, at the head of the great lakes, and last summer extended as a 30-inch line capable of carrying 300,000 barrels a day to Sarnia in southwestern Ontario. Then there is the Trans Mountain pipe line, built from Edmonton to Vancouver, which will be extended to supply refineries in the state of Washington. If present plans for gas pipe lines are fulfilled, as seems now probable, the next two or three years should witness a very large pipe line building program, with gas eventually moving eastward from southern Alberta to supply central Canada, and gas moving from the Peace river area to supply Vancouver and the Pacific coast area of United States.
I wish now, Mr. Chairman, to say something on the activities of the metal mining industry.
Iron ore production showed an increase of over one million short tons over 1952 to a total of 6,501,000 tons as a result of the expansion under way at properties in northwestern Ontario, Newfoundland and British Columbia. The steady growth of the industry in these provinces, and particularly in northwestern Ontario, is expected to raise production this year to well over the seven million ton mark. This is without the addition of output from the Knob Lake iron ore field in Quebec-Labrador and the Marmora property in southeastern Ontario, both of which are expected to enter production later this year.
Two areas shared the spotlight in the search for and development of uranium properties. The Beaverlodge area of northern Saskatchewan proved a hive of activity with several companies carrying out pre-production development work on their properties. Feverish staking in the district of Algoma in northern Ontario followed a uranium strike near Blind River, about halfway between Sudbury and Sault Ste. Marie, and thousands of claims were staked during the latter half of 1953, and diamond drilling and surface development work is under way.
A huge development program involving hundreds of millions of dollars is now under way to expand nickel-producing facilities in the Sudbury area from which comes 85 per cent of the world output of nickel. In
19, 1954	3177
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys addition to the expansion under way by the two major producers, three new companies entered production in the area in 1953. Output increased 6-8 million pounds over 1952 to a total of 287-9 million pounds, and this is expected to reach 320 million pounds this year. This will include production from the Lynn Lake nickel-copper mine in northern Manitoba.
These are only a few of the highlights of Canadian mining in 1953 but they are indicative of an industry that is rapidly going places. Such growth, as is to be expected, has been attended by many and varied problems in mining and metallurgy, which in turn have led to considerable increase in the demands made upon the services available in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. These services range from topographical and geological surveys to metallurgical assistance in the extraction of metals and minerals from ores, and they include research into the preparation, bene-ficiation and utilization of the products of the Canadian mining and metal industries.
By steadily expanding its services the department is making every effort to keep pace with the increasingly heavy demands made upon it by a rapidly growing industry. As a consequence, it has been necessary to plan for new laboratory construction; and we hope that construction will start soon. This includes a building that will provide accommodation for mines branch research work on uranium ores and minerals, for its chemical laboratories and for offices for its administrative staff. Also a new building is needed in which to house the geological survey. The construction of a geophysical laboratory will shortly be started to provide space for three divisions of the dominion observatory.
The department comprises five branches: the surveys and mapping branch, the geological survey of Canada, the mines branch, the dominion observatories and the geographical branch.
The surveys and mapping branch produces the maps, aeronautical charts and hydrographic charts necessary for the development and administration of the country and for its defence. The continuing high rate of natural resources development, with no slackening in defence requirements, caused a strong demand for new maps and charts. Including geological maps, almost one million maps and charts were distributed during 1953.
The surveys and mapping branch placed 70 parties in the field in 1953 to carry out geodetic, topographic and legal surveys work. Approximately the same number will be
3178	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys sent into the field in 1954. In addition to the regular parties, winter field parties are being used to excellent advantage as they can penetrate into areas which are practically inaccessible during any other season of the year.
In co-operation with the Royal Canadian Air Force, the national research council and the meteorological service of the Department of Transport, the branch continued to cover the far north with shoran trilateration, a new electronic method of measuring long distances on the earth's surface, which permits the extension of control into remote areas much more speedily than by conventional methods of triangulation. Since 1948 when this method was first put into use, the sparsely settled area south of the Arctic archipelago, with the exception of Yukon, has been fairly well covered with shoran trilateration.
It is hoped that this method can be extended, in the coming years, with the assistance of the R.C.A.F., to bridge across from the mainland to cover the southern part of the Arctic archipelago. Some triangulation and precise levelling has been and will continue to be done by the geodetic survey for the St. Lawrence seaway project, and triangulation work will include the area of the Hamilton river on the coast of Labrador.
Using helicopters the topographic survey did topographical mapping over 20,740 square miles of territory in northern Quebec-Labrador in the important mineralized region between Knob Lake and Fort Chimo, about 20 miles south of Ungava bay. Two other helicopter-supported operations are planned for next summer. One of these will operate in the Hamilton river watershed and will assist in providing control data for assessment of power development possibilities along that river and particularly at Grand falls.
A little more work by the topographic survey this coming summer in Newfoundland will complete the horizontal and vertical controls needed to map the province. It is hoped that the island portion of Newfoundland will be fully mapped at the one-mile scale within the next two or three years.
The house will be asked to vote the sum of $1,500,000 for the construction of a new hydrographic ship to ply in northern waters. A great amount of work remains to be done to chart our Arctic seas. As a matter of fact, it will go on for perhaps a hundred years. New and forthcoming mining developments in northern Canada require the charting of new sea routes and of approaches to potential


harbour sites, particularly in Ungava bay, where vast reserves of iron ore have been discovered.
The geological survey of Canada investigates and studies the geology of Canada, thereby assisting in the search for and development of mineral deposits. It also studies ground water supplies, makes soil surveys and investigates bedrock conditions relative to construction project problems. In 1953 it had 79 parties in the field and it expects to send probably 87 parties into the field in 1954.
The possibility that oil may exist in commercial quantities in the northwestern Arctic islands came to light as a result of the geological survey's field work in 1953 on a prominent circular structure on Ellef Ringnes island. Air photographs have revealed several such structures on these islands. These structures appear to be similar to the salt domes in the oil fields of Texas and Louisiana, many of which have formed traps for highly productive oil pools.
In 1954, it is proposed to undertake an airborne geological reconnaissance survey in the area lying west of Hudson bay and east of Great Slave lake. This survey is identified as "Operation Baker" and is an extension of "Operation Keewatin" which was conducted in the same general area in 1952. Plans are being made for another extension- "Operation Thelon" for 1955. The survey thus hopes to map the entire area between latitudes 60 and 65 and between Hudson bay and Great Slave lake by the end of 1955.
The office maintained by the geological survey of Canada in Calgary, Alberta, gave special attention to the study of oil and gas structures in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. In its office at Sydney, Nova Scotia, the survey continued to make a microscopic study of coal particularly for correlation of coal seams. These two offices in Calgary and Sydney will continue their work throughout the coming fiscal year; also the offices in Vancouver and Yellowknife will continue to serve the public. The intensive interest in prospecting for uranium resulted in the radiometric assay of approximately 1,200 samples by the radioactivity resources division of the geological survey. The division revised and published a second edition of 5,000 copies of the handbook, "Prospecting for Uranium in Canada". It is expected that this division will be even busier in the coming year with the intensified search for and discovery of uranium deposits.
An airborne aeromagnetic survey will be conducted next summer in that region north of Beaverlodge and extending into the North-

west Territories, in the hope of delimiting the northward extent of the Beaverlodge uranium-bearing geological formations.
The activities of our mines branch are directly concerned with the technological problems of the mining and metal industry and the branch maintains well equipped laboratories for tests, investigative work and research on these problems in the buildings down on Booth street. If any hon. members have the spare time, we would be very pleased to have them go down there and see what is being done.
The following are some of the highlights of mines branch activities during 1953. Forty-four reports were made to organizations submitting bulk ore samples for testing. Those on the treatment of ores from new properties included, when requested, recommendations for the design of flow sheets for the milling plants. A number of shipments were received from operating properties, and reports on these included recommendations for improving the treatment of the ores and reducing operating costs. Work in 1954 will include studies on the treatment of the complex New Brunswick ores of the Bathurst area.
Research was continued with encouraging results on the baffling problem of producing titanium metal of high purity at costs which would permit its wider use in industry. The development of an efficient economic process would mean that the large deposits of ilme-nite at Allard Lake in Quebec would become an important source of the metal. This research will be continued in 1954.
